claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution.
Elements are distributed fairly homogeneously in the initial state.
Thermal exposure induces a diffusion-mediated transformation of the metastable solid solution.
The diffusion-mediated transformation forms discrete intermetallic compounds at and near grain boundaries.
Thermal activation drives diffusion and decomposition of the metastable solid solution into equilibrium phases.
Intermetallic precipitates coarsen and become interconnected during thermal exposure.
Coarsened, interconnected intermetallic compounds create continuous pathways that undermine protective surface films.
Undermining the protective surface films reduces corrosion resistance.
Undermining the protective surface films reduces high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Aged samples containing interconnected intermetallic phases will have poorer corrosion resistance than the initial metastable state.
Aged samples containing interconnected intermetallic phases will have poorer oxidation resistance than the initial metastable state.
Samples in which intermetallics remain isolated or minimal will retain better protective behavior than samples with interconnected intermetallics.
The proposed service regime is sustained exposure at 400–600°C.
Temperatures of 400–600°C are sufficient to activate diffusion in the alloy without melting its matrix.
The relevant exposure times permit diffusion but do not allow complete equilibration.
The controlled comparison is between minimally aged samples retaining the initial metastable state and samples aged at 400°C, 500°C, or 600°C for varying durations.
The hypothesis is falsified if aging does not significantly form or coarsen intermetallic compounds.

The hypothesis is falsified if observable intermetallic connectivity is not accompanied by a statistically significant reduction in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the baseline.
